rows.description: A toddler pours sand from cup to cup for a long stretch, deaf to calls for lunch. Total absorption in a task of the right size is the earliest form of flow, and being pulled out abruptly can bring tears.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A child lost in assembling blocks or drawing forgets hunger, time and even the wish for praise. The task is just hard enough to hold attention and easy enough to keep going.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A child deep in a drawing is called for an errand and reacts with sudden irritation. The anger is real grief at a broken state, not rudeness, and a five-minute warning usually prevents it.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A parent sees a teenager absorbed for hours and cannot tell whether it is flow or compulsion. The difference shows afterward: flow leaves a person energised and having grown, while capture leaves them drained and restless.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager learns to silence notifications and set a fixed block for deep work or practice. Flow needs about fifteen unbroken minutes to arrive, and guarding that window is a skill, not stubbornness.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 23–26

rows.description: A coworker sees a teammate gone silent and intense at their desk and waits before interrupting. Recognising flow in others and holding non-urgent questions is a quiet form of respect.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 7–12, 13–17

rows.description: A toddler bangs pots, splashes water and drops spoons repeatedly to see what happens. This is not mischief but experimentation, and the repetition is how cause and effect is learned.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child runs a make-believe shop or hospital, assigning roles and correcting others who break the story. Pretend play rehearses adult life, emotions and rules in a safe frame.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A parent who follows the child's lead in play, rather than directing it, gives the child a sense of authority and being enjoyed. Taking a small role and letting the child write the story builds trust.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A child standing at the edge of a game, waiting to be asked, feels exposed and small. Some invite themselves in bravely, others drift away, and a friendly peer or adult noticing changes the afternoon.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 18–22, 23–26
